summary:
The Republic of Tyva (Tuva) stands under the national framework of Russia, and no division-specific transgender evidence appears in the source inventory for this republic; a trans visitor is assessed against the countrywide regime as it operates in Tuva.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition are banned: the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court of Russia designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the framework this division is assessed against. That note records that between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, that 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) alongside detention of up to 15 days, and that the note contains no information specific to Tuva beyond the national framework.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participation in the International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. The same report documents 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. Human Rights Watch records no Tuva-specific detail, and this national enforcement baseline applies to the republic.

Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this explicitly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.
tangentialFactors:
The scope of the crackdown is national and has grown in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, with fines under those statutes bringing more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation response was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Guardian's account concerns the capital, not Tuva, but it evidences how quickly the designation converted into raid activity.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
localsOnly:
Russian residents and nationals face the domestic penalties attached to these statutes. 'Gay propaganda' fines for individuals run to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and administrative liability under article 20.3 covers display of banned LGBT symbols, most often posted on social media; 81 people were found guilty in 98 such cases since January 2024.

Criminal extremism charges carry up to 12 years in prison, and 101 convictions have been issued since the November 2023 designation. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are unavailable to residents: the 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal changes of gender on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned that year.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports transgender-specific violence, arrests, raids, health-service access or police conduct in the Republic of Tyva itself. The division-specific position is unresolved: the UK Home Office note explicitly states that it contains no information beyond the national framework, and the Human Rights Watch article carries no Tuva detail.

Whether Tyva's regional authorities have issued their own public statements or enforcement instructions on LGBT issues, and whether local courts have handled extremism or article 20.3 cases in the republic, is not sourced here and remains unverified.

The count of 101 extremism convictions and 98 article 20.3 cases is reported as a national total with no territorial breakdown available, so the share attributable to this republic cannot be established from these sources.
